title: 5.6 Compatibility of Aerobic and Anaerobic Modes of Training

cards.tag: The Interference Effect & Power vs. Strength
cards.front: How does concurrent aerobic endurance and resistance training affect maximal power output compared to slow-velocity strength?
cards.back: Explosive power development and rate of force development (RFD) are significantly more compromised by concurrent training than slow-velocity maximal strength (1RM), due to opposing neural signaling and myofibrillar protein alterations.

cards.front: Does heavy resistance training negatively affect maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) or endurance performance?
cards.back: No. Heavy resistance exercise generally has no adverse effects on VO2max or aerobic power, and instead serves to enhance endurance performance by improving movement economy and work capacity.

cards.front: What unique aerobic development outcome was reported by Kraemer et al. in female athletes performing concurrent training?
cards.back: Women who performed combined resistance and aerobic endurance training achieved greater aerobic development (VO2max gains) than those who performed aerobic endurance training alone.

cards.front: How do heavy resistance training and high-intensity aerobic interval training compare in driving Type IIx to Type IIa fiber transformation?
cards.back: Heavy resistance training drives a near-complete transformation of Type IIx fibers to Type IIa (e.g., 19.1% down to 1.9%), whereas aerobic interval training results in a smaller reduction (e.g., 19.2% down to 8.8%), proving that heavy lifting recruits a larger pool of high-threshold Type IIx fibers.

cards.front: How does concurrent training alter fiber-specific hypertrophy compared to resistance training alone?
cards.back: Resistance training alone increases muscle fiber cross-sectional area across Type I, Type IIa, and Type IIc fibers. Concurrent training selectively restricts hypertrophy to Type IIa fibers only, blocking Type I fiber hypertrophy.

cards.front: Why does aerobic endurance training alone induce atrophy in Type I and Type IIc muscle fibers?
cards.back: Aerobic endurance training elevates catabolic cortisol levels (while reducing testosterone) and creates a physiological demand for shorter capillary-to-cell diffusion distances to optimize oxygen kinetics.

cards.front: Why does high-frequency concurrent training (e.g., 6 consecutive days/week) impair strength and power development?
cards.back: Training on 6 consecutive days per week triggers systemic overtraining mechanisms due to inadequate recovery between opposing neural and metabolic stress stimuli.

cards.front: According to Sale et al., how does training on separated days (4 days/week) compare to same-day combined workouts (2 days/week) for leg press 1RM gains?
cards.back: Training on separated days (2 days strength, 2 days endurance) yielded a 25% increase in leg press 1RM, compared to only 13% when both modes were combined into the same workout sessions.

cards.front: How does performing a 25-minute aerobic workout 30 minutes prior to resistance training affect squatting performance?
cards.back: Prior aerobic exercise reduces squat repetition performance by 13% to 36% across sets due to acute glycogen depletion and localized neuromuscular fatigue.

cards.front: How does concurrent training affect the rate of force development (RFD) compared to resistance training alone?
cards.back: Resistance training alone significantly increases the rate of force development (RFD), whereas concurrent training blunts or completely prevents improvements in RFD and explosive muscle power.
